title: Rama follows a guru
hook: the sage Vishvamitra; the bow no one can lift

segments.voice: Yesterday: putrakameshti, the fire ritual, and Vishnu born as Rama. Avatar: God comes down. Today, the boy who is God has to learn, and leave home to do it.

Four brothers grow up in a palace. Rama and Lakshmana are inseparable; so are Bharata and Shatrughna. Then a famous sage walks into the court: Vishvamitra. Demons keep ruining his sacrifices in the forest, and he wants help. Not the army. Not the king. He wants Rama, who is, the text says, not yet sixteen. Dasharatha, who waited so long for this boy, panics. Take my army, take me, he says, just not my son. The family priest, Vasishtha, gently tells him: let him go. He'll be safe with this teacher, and he'll need what he learns.
screen: `FOUR BROTHERS.` → `THE SAGE WANTS RAMA.` → `NOT YET SIXTEEN.` → `LET HIM GO.`

segments.voice: So Rama and Lakshmana follow the sage into the forest. In the tradition, Rama is Vishnu born human, and still he has to learn. On a riverbank the sage teaches the boys two mantras, bala and atibala, so they won't feel hunger or tiredness, and later he gives Rama divine weapons. Rama guards the sage's sacrifice and drives the demons off. One demon, Maricha, is hurled far out into the sea by a single arrow, and survives. Hold on to his name; he'll be back. This is the bond Hindus call guru and shishya, teacher and student. Guru is often explained as the one who removes darkness, and a guru gives more than facts: a mantra, a way of living, courage. That's why many Hindus touch a teacher's feet, why there's a day each year to honor teachers, Guru Purnima, and why in many families a child's first letters begin with a prayer and a teacher's hand guiding theirs. If God, born as a prince, still walked behind a teacher, nobody is too grand to learn. Then the sage takes them to Mithila. In King Janaka's court sits a bow that once belonged to Shiva himself, so heavy, in Valmiki's telling, that it's wheeled in on an iron cart dragged by thousands of men. Not one king could even lift it. Whoever strings it may marry Janaka's daughter, Sita. Rama walks up and lifts it as if it were nothing. Tomorrow: what happens when he tries to string it.
screen: `GOD, BORN HUMAN, STILL LEARNS.` · `BALA AND ATIBALA: TWO MANTRAS.` · `GURU AND SHISHYA.` · `SHIVA'S BOW: RAMA LIFTS IT.` · then, large: `EVEN RAMA NEEDED A GURU.`

segments.voice: In many Hindu homes you greet a teacher by bowing, palms together, or by touching their feet. Picture one teacher who changed you: a grandparent, a coach, a guru. Put your palms together, bow your head a little, and thank them by name. If you don't pray, just say their name and what they gave you.
Vishvamitra, the sage who takes Rama into the forest. Rama leaves home with him, learns to fight, and lifts Shiva's bow in Janaka's court when no one else could.
Your line: even Rama needed a guru. If God, born human, walked behind a teacher, so can you. Day thirty-seven, done.

howItsDone: Rama's youth, his journey with Vishvamitra and the lifting of Shiva's bow are favorite scenes in Ramlila plays and in children's retellings of the Ramayana.
